items.question_text: A 58-year-old woman attends a Melbourne general practice on a Thursday afternoon for a repeat of transdermal oestradiol, which she has used since a surgical menopause at 49. She works as a school registrar, walks to the station each day, and has no chest pain, breast lump, nipple discharge, skin dimpling, or axillary swelling. Her mother is alive at 84 and has never had cancer. An aunt had breast cancer at 71 and is also alive. She took the oral contraceptive pill for less than a year in her twenties, had two children before 30, and breastfed both. She drinks a glass of wine on weekends and has never smoked. Her last BreastScreen report, 26 months ago, was normal and described heterogeneously dense tissue. She has spent the week reading online forums in which women with dense breasts were told that mammography is almost useless and that they should pay for a private contrast MRI every year. A private radiologist who imaged her shoulder last year made a similar offhand comment about density. She is worried that density means the mammogram missed something, and she asks whether she should abandon the program and book a private contrast MRI instead. Her BMI is 27. Examination of both breasts and axillae is normal. There is no skin change and no nipple retraction. She takes no other medicines and has no implants. A recent full blood count, done for fatigue that resolved, was normal. She is not on an anticoagulant. Her blood pressure today is 128/76. She is not diabetic. A cholesterol check last month was acceptable. She can attend a screening centre within two weeks. Her GP notes that she is squarely inside the invited age band and that her family history does not meet criteria for a familial cancer clinic. She has capacity, is not pregnant, and asks, plainly, what she should actually do this year. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now
Arrange annual breast MRI as her population screening test
Replace mammography with screening ultrasound because the last report mentioned density
Defer all imaging until 65 because the last mammogram was normal
Measure CA 15-3 today and screen only if it is raised
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A symptom-free 58-year-old who is 26 months past a normal mammogram is due for BreastScreen mammography, not MRI or ultrasound prompted by density or an aunt's cancer.

2. THE RULE
BreastScreen invitation and who may attend

3. WHY THIS OPTION
A matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
She is symptom-free, 58, and 26 months past a normal mammogram, so she is due for the BreastScreen test. Heterogeneous density and an aunt diagnosed at 71 do not move her onto MRI. Hormone therapy is not a reason to change the program test.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Invite a symptom-free woman aged 50–74 to BreastScreen every 2 years.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
BreastScreen invites women aged 50–74 for mammography every 2 years.

---

items.question_text: A 46-year-old woman in Adelaide has asked the receptionist for a BreastScreen referral after a friend said free mammograms do not start until 50 and that asking earlier is a waste of everyone's time. She has no lump, pain, nipple change, or skin thickening. Her sister had a fibroadenoma excised at 29. There is no relative with breast or ovarian cancer. She is otherwise well, has never had breast imaging, had one child at 32, and breastfed for four months. She works in a call centre, does not smoke, and drinks rarely. She is anxious because a colleague was diagnosed at 48, and she has convinced herself that waiting until 50 is reckless. On examination both breasts are normal, with no axillary nodes. She is not pregnant. She asks whether booking now is pointless, whether she will be turned away, and whether she should instead pay for a private ultrasound to be safe. A local radiology group has already quoted her $480 for a bilateral ultrasound and mammogram. Her GP records show no breast complaint in six years at the practice. There is no chest-wall radiation in her history. A cousin had a benign cyst drained at 40. She has private health insurance and wants a clear answer on whether the public system will accept her at 46. Blood pressure is 122/74. She takes no regular medicines. A recent cervical screen was normal. She can attend a centre next week if advised. Examination today adds nothing. What is the most appropriate advice about BreastScreen?  She has never used hormone therapy. Her periods stopped at 44. There is no personal history of atypical hyperplasia or lobular carcinoma in situ. A maternal grandmother died of unrelated heart disease at 80. She is up to date with cervical screening. The receptionist has already told her the referral will be rejected, which is why she is asking the GP directly. She is prepared to pay privately if the public pathway is closed to her, but she would prefer not to. The examination adds no mass, no skin change, and no node. The decision is whether a 46-year-old asymptomatic woman can attend BreastScreen now.
options: Tell her she is ineligible for a free mammogram until she turns 50
She can book a BreastScreen mammogram now, but she will not be routinely invited until 50
Start annual mammography from today until 74 because she has asked early
Screen with ultrasound every year until she enters the invitation group
A normal examination today replaces imaging until 50

items.question_text: A 61-year-old woman in Brisbane notices a new hard lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast while showering. It has been there for three weeks. She had a normal BreastScreen mammogram 14 months ago. There is no nipple discharge. She is a non-smoker, takes perindopril for hypertension, and has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination there is a 2 cm firm, irregular mass, tethered to skin, with a palpable left axillary node. She is frightened and asks whether she should simply wait for her next BreastScreen invitation, which she believes is the proper pathway, or book the routine screening mammogram a few months early. Her sister has told her that screening clinics are faster than hospital clinics. She has no fever, no recent trauma, and no signs of infection. The remainder of the examination is normal. She is systemically well, weight stable, and has no bone pain. A BreastScreen letter from 14 months ago is in her bag and is normal. The axillary node is firm and about 1.5 cm. She is post-menopausal on no hormone therapy. Her sister has offered to drive her to a BreastScreen van in the suburb next week. The GP can feel the mass and the node. Bloods last month were unremarkable. She is not anticoagulated. What is the most appropriate next step?  She noticed the lump on a Saturday and has checked it daily since. It has not changed with her cycle because she no longer has cycles. There is no nipple inversion of long standing. A previous cyst was aspirated on the other side ten years ago and did not recur. She is a non-drinker. Her last mammogram report, which she has brought, says no significant abnormality and BIRADS 1. The node in the axilla was not present at her last GP visit six months ago for a flu vaccine. She is afebrile. There is no erythema. Weight is stable at 68 kg. The question is whether a new mass with a node goes to screening or to diagnostic assessment.
options: Use the BreastScreen appointment and review her once the screening report returns
Reassure her that a mobile lump under 45 can be reviewed in 6 months
Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram
Start tamoxifen now and image only if the lump is still there in 3 months
Request CA 15-3 and a chest X-ray as the first screen
items.explanation:

C. Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

---

A 3-week hard breast lump needs diagnostic triple assessment. A convenient BreastScreen slot does not convert it into a screening episode.

2. THE RULE
Breast symptom or high risk is not routine BreastScreen

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
A new hard lump is a symptom. BreastScreen is for women without breast symptoms, and a screening slot does not investigate a palpable mass. She needs diagnostic triple assessment: clinical review, diagnostic imaging, and needle biopsy as indicated.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT

9. RELATED RULES

10. MEMORY ANCHOR

items.question_text: A 77-year-old woman in Hobart has not been invited to BreastScreen for two years. She is well, has no breast symptom, and had normal screens throughout her sixties. Her daughter has read that screening stops at 74 and has told her she is no longer allowed to attend. She is a retired teacher, lives alone, drives, and has no cognitive impairment. There is no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. She takes a statin and vitamin D. Examination is normal. She asks whether the program has closed to her permanently, whether attending would be against the rules, and whether she should instead pay for a private mammogram every year for the rest of her life. She is not frail, has a life expectancy well beyond a few years, and can consent for herself. Her GP is aware that invitation and access are not the same thing at this age.  She has attended BreastScreen regularly since 52 and has every normal report in a folder at home. Her daughter read a news article saying the program ends at 74 and has booked her a private annual mammogram at $320 a time. She is a retired teacher, lives alone, drives, and manages her own medicines. There is no cognitive impairment. She takes atorvastatin and vitamin D only. There is no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Examination today is normal, with no mass and no node. She is not frail. Her GP estimates her life expectancy is well beyond five years. She asks whether the program has closed to her permanently, whether attending would be against the rules, and whether private imaging every year is now her only option. She can consent for herself. The question is invitation versus access after 74. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Further mammography is contraindicated once she is over 74
She must continue annual mammography until 80 to stay enrolled
Transfer her to annual screening MRI because invitation has stopped
She is no longer invited, but she may choose to book BreastScreen after a discussion of benefit
Replace mammography with 2-yearly clinical examination only

---

BreastScreen invitation and who may attend

3. WHY THIS OPTION

Active invitation stops after 74. That is not a ban. A well 76-year-old with no breast symptoms may choose to keep attending after a discussion of benefit, overdiagnosis, and competing health problems. Her last screen was 18 months ago, so she is not even due today.

Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
She is no longer invited, but she may choose to book BreastScreen after a discussion of benefit

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES

items.question_text: A 42-year-old woman is found to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 variant after her sister died of ovarian cancer at 46. She has no breast symptom. She has been told by a relative to just join BreastScreen early and have an ordinary mammogram every two years like everyone else. She has two children, breastfed both, does not smoke, and has not had risk-reducing surgery. She is anxious, has been reading conflicting advice online, and asks whether the national screening program is enough now that the gene result is known. Examination of breasts and axillae is normal. She is not pregnant. There is no lump. Her GP has the genetic report. A colleague suggests that because she is under 50 she cannot access any imaging at all, and another suggests a single private ultrasound and discharge.  The BRCA1 result arrived last week from a familial cancer service that tested her after her sister's death. She has no breast symptom, no ovarian symptom, and has not had risk-reducing surgery. She has two children, breastfed both, and does not smoke. A relative has told her to join BreastScreen early and have an ordinary mammogram every two years. She has been reading conflicting advice online, some of it about MRI and some about ultrasound. Examination of breasts and axillae is normal. She is not pregnant. There is no lump. Her GP has the genetic report in the file. A colleague has suggested she is too young for any imaging, and another has suggested a single private ultrasound and discharge. She is anxious and wants to know if the national program is enough now that the gene is known. The pathway is not routine screening. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Routine BreastScreen from age 50 is sufficient for a BRCA1 carrier
Population ultrasound from age 30 can replace specialist review during pregnancy
Bilateral mastectomy must be booked before any further imaging or pregnancy care
Defer every breast decision until she has finished childbearing
Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
BRCA1 is not covered by waiting for BreastScreen at 50. She should be referred to a familial cancer service, not booked for immediate mastectomy.

2. THE RULE
Breast symptom or high risk is not routine BreastScreen

3. WHY THIS OPTION
E matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
A pathogenic BRCA1 variant is not average risk, and pregnancy does not park that fact until BreastScreen invitation at 50. She needs a familial cancer service to plan surveillance, usually earlier and with MRI considered. Surgery may be discussed later. It is not an emergency order before antenatal care.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
A known high-risk mutation needs a familial pathway, not routine BreastScreen alone.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR

---
